issues.legal_issue: An accused’s failure to explain incriminating circumstances in the examination following the prosecution evidence may support an adverse inference where those circumstances call for an explanation.
material_facts: The accused did not deny visiting the complainant’s home and staying there, and did not explain the visit.
Treated currency was recovered from the pocket of the accused’s trousers, and his hands and part of his trousers turned pink when washed.
When questioned about the incriminating circumstances, the accused gave no explanation for them.
issues.conclusion: The court was entitled to draw an adverse inference from the accused’s failure to explain the incriminating circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an accused may remain silent or deny the allegations, but the court may draw an adverse inference permissible by law when the accused gives no explanation for incriminating material put to him. The court relied on Ramnaresh & Ors. v. State of Chhattisgarh, AIR 2012 SC 1357; Munish Mubar v. State of Haryana, AIR 2013 SC 912; and Raj Kumar Singh alias Raju @ Batya v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 2013 SC 3150.

predicates.criminal_trial_with_accused_examined_on_: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the accused is examined about incriminating evidence.
predicates.incriminating_circumstances_call_for_exp: The prosecution evidence presents circumstances against the accused that call for an explanation.
predicates.accused_offers_no_explanation: The accused gives no explanation for those circumstances when examined.

issues.definition: When an accused in a criminal trial gives no explanation for incriminating circumstances that call for one, an adverse inference may be drawn.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal only in exceptional circumstances where there are compelling reasons and the acquittal judgment is perverse, and it should not interfere merely because another view is possible.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, and the High Court reversed that acquittal after considering the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court’s judgment was based on the evidence and that the evidence had been properly reappreciated.
The Supreme Court found no perversity in the High Court’s judgment warranting further interference.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s reversal of the acquittal did not warrant interference, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court must bear in mind the presumption of innocence, which is strengthened by an acquittal, and should avoid routine interference when another view is possible. In exceptional cases, compelling circumstances and perversity in the judgment under appeal permit appellate interference.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.compelling_circumstances_exist: The circumstances of the case provide compelling reasons for appellate intervention.

issues.definition: In an appeal from an acquittal, appellate interference is permitted when compelling circumstances exist and the acquittal judgment is perverse.
